item.title: Font Converters Earns a 49.57 Proof of Usefulness Score by Building a Lossless, Privacy-First Font Pipeline
item.content:encoded: Font Converters is a free, privacy-first web tool that turns one font into all the formats you actually need, converting losslessly between the 8 major font formats and generating the matching @font-face CSS. It also re-sets whole documents (PDF, DOCX, and more) in any font, including OpenDyslexic for accessibility, and bundles utilities like a font analyzer, subsetter, and license checker. There's no account, and everything you upload is deleted the moment the conversion finishes. Around 1,500 people a month find it through organic search alone, with roughly 1,200 returning, and the focus now is growing the underserved accessibility and licensing tools that bigger converters ignore.

item.title: A Practical Security Architecture for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
item.content:encoded: This article argues that the primary security risks in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems often originate in the retrieval layer rather than the language model itself. Drawing on real-world experience, the author outlines a layered security architecture that includes structural prompt separation, corpus sanitization, retrieval-level access controls, tool-layer enforcement, tenant isolation, and observability safeguards. The central thesis is that secure RAG systems are built by limiting what untrusted content can influence and what models are allowed to do after retrieval.

item.title: Fraud Detection Isn't a Machine Learning Problem
item.content:encoded: This article argues that fraud detection should be viewed as a decision-support system rather than a standalone machine learning problem. While model metrics such as precision, recall, and AUC remain important, the author emphasizes that real-world fraud prevention depends on operational workflows, behavioral analytics, threshold management, explainability, monitoring, and analyst usability. The central thesis is that the most effective fraud systems optimize for decision quality and business outcomes—not just predictive performance.

item.title: A Framework-Agnostic Approach to SSR for Microfrontends
item.content:encoded: After struggling to add SSR to a microfrontend architecture without introducing shared builds or centralized orchestration, the author created @mf-toolkit/mf-ssr. The article explains the architectural decisions behind the project, including support for both server-rendered remotes and static bundle remotes, framework-agnostic communication patterns, DOM-based prop synchronization, streaming SSR, edge-runtime compatibility, and failure-handling strategies. The goal is to enable independently deployed microfrontend teams to achieve server-side rendering benefits without sacrificing deployment autonomy.

item.title: From Overwhelming CI Logs to Fix Plans: Rethinking TypeScript Dependency Scans
item.content:encoded: Most dependency scanners tell developers what is vulnerable, but not clearly enough what to fix next. TypeScript projects need local, remediation-first workflows that separate direct and transitive risks, explain dependency paths, and verify fixes before CI becomes the first warning.

item.title: Why Vulnerability Reduction Percentages Can Be Misleading
item.content:encoded: This article examines the reality behind vulnerability reduction claims commonly cited in cybersecurity reporting. Drawing on firsthand experience, the author explains how factors such as false-positive triage, risk acceptance, platform upgrades, remediation work, and prevention initiatives all contribute to reported improvements. The piece argues that while large vulnerability reductions can represent meaningful security gains, headline percentages often obscure the underlying complexity, costs, incentives, and tradeoffs involved in improving software security programs.

item.title: Building a Production Pipeline for Prompt Evaluation and Regression Testing
item.content:encoded: This article presents a production-ready framework for managing prompt changes in LLM applications. Using prompt repositories, replay datasets, automated evaluators, Phoenix tracing, promotion gates, and canary deployments, the author shows how teams can detect behavioral regressions before users experience them. The central argument is that prompts should be treated as operational artifacts rather than text strings, with the same rigor applied to testing, deployment, observability, and rollback strategies as traditional software releases.

item.title: Exploring the History and Psychology of Precognition
item.content:encoded: Using a personal family story as a starting point, this article examines the concept of precognition and humanity's long-standing fascination with predicting future events. The author explores historical government research programs such as Project Stargate, theories surrounding remote viewing and altered states of consciousness, and alternative explanations rooted in psychology, pattern recognition, and intuition. Ultimately, the piece argues that what people describe as precognition may be less about literally seeing the future and more about the mind's ability to identify patterns and influence outcomes through belief, attention, and action.

item.content:encoded:
Calling ClamAV from Node.js looks easy: spawn clamscan, check the exit code, done. But the standard implementation has a silent bug — exit code 2 means "scan could not complete," not "clean," and almost every custom wrapper collapses it into one of the other two outcomes. The result is a false-clean verdict on encrypted archives, permission-denied files, and timeouts. The fix is to model ClamAV's three real outcomes — Clean, Malicious, ScanError — as three explicit return values, and force the caller to handle ScanError as a security decision rather than a programming error. This article explains why this matters, what the failure looks like in production, and what a correct minimal wrapper looks like in practice.
